Sound environmental management ................................ ................................ ................................ ........... 41 4 DG DEFIS IN BRIEF The mission of the Directorate - General for Defence Industry and Space (DG DEFIS) is to lead the implementation of EU defence industry and space policies and programmes , supporting European strategic autonomy and security, while advancing defence and space capability development through innovative technologies, industrial competitiveness, and cross - sector syne

mes , supporting European strategic autonomy and security, while advancing defence and space capability development through innovative technologies, industrial competitiveness, and cross - sector synergies . EU competences and obligations for defence in dustry action are conferred under the TFEU Title XVII Industry, in particular Article 173(3), and Title XIX Research and development, in particular Article 182(4), Article 183 and the second paragraph of Article 188; and for space under Articles 189 and 4( 3) TFEU. The policy domains of the defence industry and space fall under shared competence with Member States , bordering areas where Member States have exclusive competences, such as security and defence. Under the leadership of European Commissioner for D efence and Space, Andrius Kubilius , DG DEFIS collaborates closely with Member States and key stakeholders to strengthen the EU's defence and space capa bilities . In the context of Russia’s war on Ukraine and shifting geopolitical dynamics, DG DEFIS ’s missio n is increasingly vital for achieving EU objectives. DG DEFIS is responsible for a total budget of EUR 26.1 billion for the period 2021 - 2027 through: ▪ the European Defence Fund (EDF) and its precursors, the European Defence Industrial Development Programme (EDIDP) and the Preparatory Action on Defence Research (PADR), the EDF and EDIDP largely implemented through d

ence Fund (EDF) and its precursors, the European Defence Industrial Development Programme (EDIDP) and the Preparatory Action on Defence Research (PADR), the EDF and EDIDP largely implemented through direct management by the Commission (mainly grants) and the PADR partially implemented through indirect management by the European Defence Agency (EDA); ▪ the Act in Support of Ammunition Production (ASAP) and the EU Defence Industry Reinforcement through Common Procurement Act (EDIRPA) for 2023 - 2025 ; ▪ the European Defence Industry Programme (EDIP ) for 2025 - 2027, extending the logic of EDIRPA and ASAP; ▪ the EU Space Programme and the EU Secure Connectivity Programme, implemented through direct management by the Commission or through indirect management by the European Union Agency for the Space Programme (EUSPA), the European Space Agency (ESA) and other entrusted entities; and ▪ Horizon Europe for Space , managed by DG DEFIS and the Health and Digital Executive Agency (HaDEA) in cooperation with DG RTD, along with indirect management by EUSPA and ESA. DG DEFIS implements the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) instrument, adopted on 27 May 2025, providing up to EUR 150 billion in long - maturity loans to help Member States accelerate defence readiness and close critical capability gaps. DG DEFIS relies on external control systems , given that most of its budget is managed ind

long - maturity loans to help Member States accelerate defence readiness and close critical capability gaps. DG DEFIS relies on external control systems , given that most of its budget is managed indirectly via entrusted entities, except for most of the EU defence programmes 1 . External auditors have validated these systems through pillar assessments, based on the Commission’s common terms of reference, wit h critical recommendations implemented before any contribution agreements with entrusted entities are signed. This setup integrates the control systems of entrusted entities into DG DEFIS' accountability chain. Beyond the risks related to the direct and in direct spending modes, DG DEFIS must consider external factors beyond its control, such as technical risks (space activity), extraordinary events (e.g., the COVID - 19 pandemic and the Russian war against Ukraine), and security risks. The work of DG DEFIS in 2025 is aligned with the 2025 Management Pl an and the strategic outlook of the Strategic Plan 2025 - 2029 , with the aim of achieving the specific objectives and contribut ing to the general objectives of the Von der Leyen Commission 2025 - 2029 term . DG DEFIS’ s programmes and policy initiatives played a crucial role in enhancing EU security, resilience, and sustainability, whilst reinforcing EU strategic autonomy and competitiveness. A. Key results and progress towards achieving the Commission’s general objectives and department's specific objectives In 2025, DG DEFIS remained at the forefront of the space domain: the Commission Communication “ A Vision for the European Space Economy ” , adopted in June, sets out the objective of positioning the European Uni on as a global space leader by 2050. The pilot edition in 202 5 of the CASSINI Space Camps initiative fostered interest in the space sector among young students to spark STEM careers and inspire educators. Furthermore, CASSINI Hackathons & Mentoring supported adults and aspiring professionals by enhancing knowledge o f space data and services to use . The six Copernicus services were operated routinely in 2025 , delivering cutting - edge and authoritative information to their various user communities. It also successfully expanded its services by opening SST Re - Entry services to non - EU users , while SST Fragmentation services to EU users continued uninterrupted . Offer ing these critical services free of charge to space operators worldwide is vital for enhancing space safety and sustainability for all space actors. Belgium, Bulgaria, Lithuania and Luxembourg paved the way to join the EU SST Partnership , which soon will count 19 (from previously 15) Member States. Preparations for an operational EU space weather service are underway, with a call for tender to procure the service to be launched in early 2026. To further enhanced preparedness and responsiveness, the physica l characteristics of NEOs will continue to be studied in depth . The implementation of the In - Space Operations and Services (ISOS) pilot mission began successfully , strengthening the European Union’s ability to act in space. DG DEFIS provided support to the Strategic Technologies for Europe Platform (STEP) by identifying space calls worth EUR 53 million for 2025 and EUR 60.2 million for 2026 – 2027. In 2025 DG DEFIS continued to shape the EU’s defence industry agenda. Following the Joint White P aper for European Defence Readiness 2030 , the Commission adopted the Preserving Peace – Defence Readiness Roadmap 2030 , setting clear objectives and milestones to strengthen Europe’s defence capacities and close investment and capabilities gaps for full defence readiness by 2030. New financial instruments and tools were mobilised in pursuit of this vision under the ReArm Eu rope plan , including the Security Action f or Europe (SAFE) . The adoption of the European Def ence Industry Programme (EDIP) will further enhance the competitiveness, responsiveness and security of supply of the European defence industrial base and promote cooperation with Ukraine . The adoption of the mini - omnibus regulation opened up new opportunities for the association of Ukraine to the EDF, deepening Ukraine’s integration into the EU defence industrial and innovation ecosystem. In 2025, two new initiatives were launched under EUDIS: the Business Accelerator and Matchmaking initiatives . The launch of the BraveTech EU initiative advanced a unified EU – Ukraine technology ecosystem , accelerat ing innovati on from development to deployment. By 2025, EUR 5.4 billion had been committed to defence R&D, supporting 225 collaborative EDF projects and positioning the EDF among the EU’s top defence R&D investors. Concrete EDF success stories are emerging, with next - generation capabilities already translating into operational use, including on the battlefield in Ukraine. In 2025, DG DEFIS established a task force to implement the new SAFE (Security Action for Europe) instrument, which entered into force on 29 May. As part of the ReArm Europe – Defence Readiness 2030 Plan , SAFE provides loans to support urgent defence investments and address critical capability gaps. Member State s interest exceeded available funds , with 19 Member States submitting n ational Defence Industry Investment Plans by 30 November, covering 691 projects, 65% of which involved joint procurement. In 2025, DG DEFIS progressed the implementation of the EU Space Strategy for Security and Defence adopted in March 2023. Key actions included setting up the EU Space Sharing and Analysis Centre (ISAC) , launching feasibility studies for a pote ntial EU Earth Observation Governmental Service, and presenting progress to Member States at a year - end workshop. Discussions with Member States and the EEAS continued to focus on improving synergies between SST and SDA, including future SST governmental s ervices under the European Competitiveness Fund. In parallel, two studies on the Earth Observation Governmental Service (EOGS) were finalised , and a pilot under the Copernicus Security Service was launched. The Copernicus data and information are aimed at achieving “policy readiness” to maximise the impact of Earth observation for EU and national policy implementation. DG DEFIS has been leading t he modernisation of Copernicus services in 2025 , integrating AI - powered analytics, enhanced data acc ess, and improved service delivery for sectors such as agriculture, forestry, and emergency response. The first - ever UN Space Sustainability Days, a joint DG DEFIS - UNOOSA capacity - building workshop, fed into deliberations of the Scientific and Technical Sub - Committee (STSC) of the Committee on the Peaceful User of Outer Space (COPUOS) and helped inform t he setup of a COPUOS STSC Expert Group on space traffic coordination. 8 DG DEFIS engaged with third countries which have shown significant interest in participating in the EU ’ s secure connectivity programme and the GOVSATCOM component of the EU space progra mme. Formal negotiations with Norway and Iceland continued in 2025 and were almost finalised, with the signature of the Agreements expected in the beginning of 2026. In 2025, the Commission also proposed to Member States to authorise the opening of formal negotiations with Ukraine for their participation in IRIS² and GOVSATCOM. he Union Secure Connectivity priority flagship, the development of multi - orbital satellite constellation IRIS² (Infrastructure for Resilience, Interconnectivity and S ecurity by Satellite) continued at full speed. Several important sub - contracts were signed with core consortium team members and key suppliers. Activities focused on consolidating the baseline for the overall system design of the IRIS² infrastructure and t o ensure a high level of security for IRIS². A preliminary market consultation was conducted to support the development of user terminals that can be used with the EU’s communication satellite systems. Significant progress was achieved in preparation for t he start of operations of GOVSATCOM , a system designed to pool and share satellite communication services with Member States and authorised users. The Commission signed contracts with five resource providers: France, Greece, Italy, Luxembourg, and Spain. B uilding on this framework, a broader range of satellite communication services, featuring secure and low - latency connectivity, will be gradually made available for governmental, defence, and commercial users. DG DEFIS has implemented a comprehensive simp lification agenda to reduce administrative burdens and streamline access to EU defence funding, thereby stimulating new investment in the European defence sector . lification agenda to reduce administrative burdens and streamline access to EU defence funding, thereby stimulating new investment in the European defence sector . In 2025, the Commission proposed several major simplification initiatives through the mini - om nibus and the Defence Readiness Omnibus . The administrative burden linked to company ownership verification has been significantly reduced by extending the validity of Ownership Control Assessments (OCAs) from 18 to 36 months. Also, EDF grant award criteria have been simplified , notably for SMEs and disruptive non - thematic calls, in order to provide simpler, faster and more flexible support t o innovators. These changes cut application documentation requirements by around half , allowing companies to save substantial time and resources. Taken together, these measures are expected to generate total cost savings exceeding EUR 100 million per year for both industry and the Commission. Under the EDF , lump - sum financing was applied to the maximum extent possible, in particular in calls targeting innovative SMEs. In parallel, work has continued to introduce simpler and leaner funding cycles to facilit ate the rapid integration of cutting - edge defence solutions into operational systems, including through agile testing and validation, enabling accelerated implementation timelines that keep pace with technological change.

In addition, all EDF projects wil l be able to use the Financial Support to Third Parties (FSTP) mechanism, further facilitating the participation of start - ups and SMEs through simplified access to funding and easier integration into collaborative projects. Building on the EDF Interim Evaluation outcomes, the combined effect of these simplifications and the shorter duration of disruptive projects will accelerate the integration of new defence solutions and enable more cost - efficient development of innovative technologies, with the potential to shorten overall timelines by up to 28 months . The EU Space Act contributes to simplification by addressing the current fragmentation of national regulatory frameworks governing space activities. By introducing a common EU framework, including mechanisms such as EU - level certification and a Union registry, it streamlines procedures for operators active across several Member States and reduces duplicative compl iance and administrative requirements. 9 B. Key conclusions on internal control and financial management DG DEFIS has systematically examined the available control results and indicators, including those from supervised entities to which it has entrusted budget implementation tasks, as well as the observations and recommendations issued by the internal auditor and the European Court of Auditors. The transition in 2025 to the Commission’s new accounting system, SUMMA, has required the adjustment to a new system and has impacted budget implementation tasks, processes and financial management activities, particularly dur ing the first part of the year. This required careful management to ensure the same data quality as in previous years. All the above elements have been assessed to determine their impact on management's assurance about the achievement of the control object ives. In conclusion, management has reasonable assurance that, overall, suitable controls are in place and working as intended; risks are being appropriately monitored and mitigated. General Obje ctive 1: A new plan for Europe’s sustainable prosperity and competitiveness Specific Objective 1.1 : Strengthen the EU’s competitiveness, resilience and autonomy through the provision of modern and well - functioning EU space assets and EU space - enabled serv ices In 2025, DG DEFIS continued the efficient implementation of the EU Space Programme w ith a view to maintaining Europe’s leadership in global space innovation and security. This included advancing Horizon Europe funding for space - related research and development, bolstering synergies with defence applications, and enhancing Europe's strategic autonomy in critical space technologies. The 21st century is the century of space, with Europe’s economy increasingly reliant on space - based systems and solutions. on space - based systems and solutions. Recognising the strategic importance of space, the Commission adopted , in June 2025 , the Com munication “ A Vision for the European Space Economy ” . The Vision sets out a strategic roadmap to position the EU as a global leader in the space economy by 2050. The Vision aims to strengthen competitiveness, autonomy, innovation, and market share through more than 40 concrete actions. To support evidence - based policymaking, the European Space Economy Thematic Account (ESETA) was launched as a joint DG DEFIS – EUROSTAT – DG JRC – ESA initiative to improve official statistics on the EU space sector. Together, thes e initiatives lay the groundwork for sustainable growth and future European space capabilities. DG DEFIS pursued a sustainable space policy with a focus on strengthening resilience and safeguarding the EU’s sovereignty and security. DG DEFIS conti nues to implement the EU approach on space traffic management (STM) through ten actions in four areas: 1) assessing STM requirements of civil and military space operators; 2) enhancing operational capabilities such as SST services and assets through the ‘ E U I ndustry and S tart - ups F orum on STM’ ; 3) developing and promoting regulatory aspects; and 4) 13 promoting the EU STM approach internationally. The STM stakeholder mechanism set up in 2023 brings the fora called for in the Joint Communication ( 5 ) into a single comprehensive structure consisting of one main group and four subgroups along the four STM areas; it facilitates regular stakeholder meetings to gather valuable inputs, ideas, and contributions. In 2025, DG DEFIS also prepared the launch of two studies of the EU Space Work Programme 2025 - 2027 on space safety with a focus on constellations and on EU contributions to a global space traffic management system, respectively. In 2025, Galileo ensured seamless, safe and secure service provision, in line with public service commitments. The Galileo constellation achieved its final configuration in February 2025 , with 24 satellites in nominal slots and 3 spare satellites. From that point onwards, the constellation will be replenished as needed, as was the case with the dual launch that took place in December 2025. In July 2025 , Galileo declared the first - ever satellite - navigation authentication service, the Galileo Open Service Navigation Message Authentication (OSNMA) , which ensures that the navigation data encoded in the Galileo signals originates from the Galileo system, increasing resilience against sp oofing attacks. The year 2025 was marked by intense work to prepare the declarations of the Galileo Open Service Full Operation al Capability (OS FOC) and the Galileo Public Regulated Service Initial Operation al Capability (PRS IOC) which are expected in the first half of 2026. In addition, the Galileo High Accuracy Service delivered excellent performance , enabling high - accuracy positioning and navigation signals for efficient routes across various transport modes (cars , public transport and boats), reducing fuel consumption and CO 2 emissions. Within the field of In - Space Operations and Services (ISOS) , the year began with the signing of the EU ISOS Joint Declaration between the European Commission, France, Germany, Luxembourg, Portugal, and Spain on 28 January 2025 , to support the deployment of the ISOS P ilot M ission in 2030 and to strengthen collaboration on ISOS. This marked a significant step towards accelerating the development of Europe's strategic capability to ‘ a ct in s pace’. The ISOS Pilot Mission is a pioneering mission that aims , by 2030 , to demonstrat e in - space services and operational capabilities, enabling European space actors to provide on - demand maintenance, life extension, upgrade s , assembly, removal and logis tic s services in space. The overall control objective is to ensure that the residual error rate affecting the relevant expenditure of 2025 remains below 2%. DEFIS’ expenditure is composed of indirectly managed procurement (space , Horizon Europe ) and grants (Horizon Europe , H2020 , EDF ), directly managed grants (EDF , ASAP, EDIRPA , EDIDP ) and procurement (secured connectivity concessio

Especially in the areas of satellite navigation and Earth observation, the programme components Galileo, EGNOS and Copernicus have become true success stories, as their services are recognised for their high quality worldwide. They ensure that Europe is independent fro m other service providers in the world, in key technologies that are essential for the EU economy and society. It is therefore of crucial importance to complete, maintain and constantly modernise the infrastructure, and to further develop the services prov ide d in line with user ex pectations and political needs. For this purpose, Europe needs to capitalise on the expertise and industrial excellence available in the EU, by creating the conditions for a prospering and competitive space sector.
